title: A hymn in Asa
hook: the hymn that opens Asa asks where the door is

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Asa, and your line was hope at dawn. What hope did you give the first minute to? Day one thousand seventy-three.

Some songs you meet in more than one room. You hear one at a wedding, then again in a car, then hummed by someone at the sink, and each time it sounds a little different. The Guru Granth Sahib has a hymn like that. A Sikh who has prayed the Japji in the morning has said it. A Sikh who has prayed the Rehras in the evening has said it. And open the Granth to the first page of Raga Asa, and there it is again, standing at the door of the whole section. Today, a hymn in Asa, and the question it asks.
screen: `ONE SONG, MORE THAN ONE ROOM.` → `MORNING, EVENING, AND ASA.` → `A HYMN AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: It's called So Dar, from its first words, that door. Guru Nanak opens with a question, given here in plain English: what is that door, what is that house, where you sit and take care of everything? A few days ago, with the string instruments, you heard part of the answer from the Japji: instruments and players beyond counting. Here it goes on. The winds sing, the waters sing, fire sings. The keepers of what's right and wrong sing. The truthful, the contented, the brave. And the hymn admits its list will never be finished: many others sing, it says, whom Nanak can't even call to mind. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't do. He never gives the door an address. No hill, no temple. Then listen to how the hymn ends, because that's the part a first hearing rushes past. That One, it says, is the King, the King over kings, and Nanak lives within that will. The question was where. The answer, in the end, is how: stand inside the will, and you're already at the door. That's why it opens Asa so well. Yesterday's raga was hope at dawn. Here, at dawn, the raga's first hymn asks where God lives and answers with a way to live the day. Asa holds more as you go on: the Patti, a hymn built on the letters of a child's writing board, and the dawn ballad itself, the Asa di Var. But the way into the section is a door, a song, and a will to live inside. A raga that greets the morning starts by asking where to stand. That's today's line: the dawn raga.
screen: `SO DAR: THAT DOOR.` · `WHAT IS THAT HOUSE?` · `WIND, WATER, FIRE, SINGING.` · `NANAK LIVES WITHIN THAT WILL.` · then, large: `THE DAWN RAGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for the singers. Sit, and let your eyes close if that's comfortable. Start with the nearest sound: your breath, a fridge humming, traffic, wind. Let each one count as a voice in that crowd at the door. Then reach a little farther for the next sound, and the next. Don't name them for long; just let each one join in. If you pray, you can say Waheguru under your breath, adding one more voice. If you don't, simply keep listening outward. Later today, play one Asa shabad, So Dar if you can find it, and listen for the list. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Asa. So Dar, that door, the hymn that opens Raga Asa, which hears all creation singing where God sits. Today's word.
Your line: the dawn raga. Once today, stop at a doorway, any door at all, and count three sounds you can hear from it. Day one thousand seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet So Dar in daily prayer: a version of it is part of the Japji, and it is sung or recited as part of the Rehras in the evening. In kirtan it is also sung as a shabad of Raga Asa.

what it means: So Dar, the hymn at the door of Asa, which answers where God lives with all creation singing.
what a scholar hears: a hymn the Granth carries in more than one place, in the Japji, in the Rehras and at the head of Raga Asa, with small differences in wording.
